utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I was informed that there was a matter to be raised by the Simatovic Defence. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just briefly. My learned friend Jordash and myself have considered the topics for the examination of the witness who is currently before the Trial Chamber and we decided that some of our topics overlapped and that is why we would like to suggest that the one hour that we requested should be allocated to the Stanisic Defence. We would then need only one hour and that would bring us to the total time requested for both Defence teams. And if the Chamber finds this proposal acceptable, I would kindly ask for these slight amendments to be made to the overall distribution of our examination time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, can the witness be escorted into the courtroom. There were two hours left for you, Mr. Jordash. You were asking for two hours, Mr. Petrovic. It's now 3:1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, I'd like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony is still binding. And Mr. Jordash will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on e-court, please, 5601. 65 ter 5601, page 46 of the English and 46 of the B/C/S, and 46 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I want to ask you about the entry, Tuesday, the 11th of August, 1992, and the entry concerning Bratunac and the "Red Berets equalling 58, they have ambition to take power and they operate under the patronage of the local priest." Do you know anything about those Red Berets operating under the patronage of the local priest?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I only heard that somewhere between Bratunac and Skelani a group of 26 of some Red Berets entered the area. People also called them Seselj's Men. As for this number of 58, I wasn't aware of that. We expelled that group of -- across the Drina very quickly because they had not come to fight. They had come to loot abandoned houses, both Muslim and Serb houses. They were thieves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did that group then, that you expelled across the Drina, conduct any military operations as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not engaged in any military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You say that they had come to loot. Did they actually loot? And if so, was the property taken across the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they took anything or not. They stole little things, not furniture or any bigger things, but rather money, small utensils, whatever they could carry in their hands. They did not have any organised means of transport that would take them across the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, on the screen, 1D03595.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What I'm going to have brought up to the screen, Mr. Milovanovic, are Supreme Defence Council minutes from the FRY. I want to ask you about something that's said during a meeting, during one of those sessions. As we can see, this is minutes from -- these are minutes from the 5th Session of the Supreme Defence Council, 7th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I want to turn, if we can, please, to page 18 of the English and 18 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, were you aware of the Supreme Defence Council and its usual makeup, the people who attended?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Councils in all countries are institutions pertaining to Defence in peacetime, whereas in war time it would be Supreme Commands. The head of that body is the president of the state. There is also prime minister, minister of the interior, the defence minister. And if the state is federal, which was also the case of FRY, the president of the republics also attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to direct your attention to the bottom of the page where Pavle Bulatovic is speaking. "Regarding these 350 pieces, I have information that the MUP of Serbia is responsible for that. It is now possible that someone is looking for an alibi in these ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go over the page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "... in these stories just as they do in the General Staff. Ceko says he's going to get a permit for his vehicle, which was probably robbed and stolen somewhere in Bosnia through the General Staff. It is possible that people are looking for an alibi. I showed two faxes to minister Sokolovic, where Tikves and Ilok are mentioned, where a commander, a Montenegrin, Zivojin Ivanovic, as a commander of a special purposes units" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the right B/C/S page be displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think we need to go to the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "... where a commander of a special purposes unit informs that a group of twenty armed people are permitted to move across the territory of Serbia and across the territory of Pljevlja. He signed as a commander of some special unit. He has got a stamp, and he gives these authorisations to himself, saying that his orders have to be executed. I asked minister Sokolovic if he knew who this was and he said he's never heard of him." Then just moving down, to save time: "We are going to have things like this happen as long as the weapons are not collected from the people and stored somewhere. But I think it will not be possible to realise this in an efficient way for the next 15 years."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the witness does not have the correct B/C/S page in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go over the page then, please, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Have you followed me so far, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that text in front of me. What you were reading, I didn't have that. Now I have a page. I don't know where you started. My page starts with "In the media, the commander of White Eagles issues an open address to President Bulatovic," I suppose that that was Momir Bulatovic who was then either the president of the FRY government or the prime minister of Montenegro, in any case, he was a member of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just have a moment. Let's -- I'll come back to that. I was told that the pages were exactly the same, but clearly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just note that the document Mr. Jordash is now working with has been admitted as P2357.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we might have that on the screen now. Let's come back to that. I do apologise, I'll find the corresponding page. Let's have on the screen instead then P-- sorry, 65 ter 5601. And page 78 of the English and 78 of the B/C/S, 78 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is dated the 18th of August, 1992, Pale. It's a meeting of the -- at the SR Presidency. And on the screen we have J000-2253. I'm interested in the suggestion or the -- what appears to be a suggestion by "Colonel Dimitrija Sibalic (Bratunac): We have obtained two combat Kragujs aircraft. We have a possibility to create a network of small airports. They are asking to be under our jurisdiction for all supplies," and so on. Do you know anything about this colonel and this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Sibalic by the name, but the family name Dimitrija is known to me. He worked at the sports airport in Bratunac which was refurbished to be able to accommodate Kraguj aircraft that can be armed and used in combat. I'm not sure that I'm familiar with the family name Sibalic. I've never heard that family name before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about this suggestion of creating a network of small airports, did that happen? Did he or anyone create, as far as you're aware, a network of small airports outside of the control of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. Yesterday I spoke about some attempts to create an improvised airfield in Podromanija at the foot of Romanija mountain. The place was just marked, the plot was marked, and that was it. That's where the work stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, just remind us: Who made that attempt?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of Republika Srpska tasked the army with that and the air force and the entire aircraft defence of Republika Srpska marked the area where the airport would be, but that was it. The airport was never built. The attempt to build an airport was a response to the Muslims' project to build an airport somewhere in the area of Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to 65 ter 5602. Same as we have on the screen, but page 51 of the English, 51 of the B/C/S, and 51 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we are looking at an entry which is dated the 15th of September, 1992, and it's Bijeljina and it's a conference in the Eastern Bosnian Corps. I'm interested in what the president of the Kalesija SO Petar Jankovic appears to be reporting. "There were 8.000 Serbs, genocide is being carried out for the second time. 70 per cent of our men have been in the trenches since May of 1992, we got out. Civilian government is made up of 5 people. I'm disappointed in the Serbian people as a whole. 80 per cent of the Serbs are fleeing. 2050 men (mostly elderly) are holding 25 kilometres of the front." Do you know anything about the situation described by Jankovic in his municipality at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting in Bijeljina dealing with the military and political issues. I did not attend. Some other generals headed by General Mladic attended. In that part of Republika Srpska, which is Posavina, Semberija, and Majevica region, throughout the war there were conflicts, firstly between the civilian authorities, i.e., the municipal authorities, and military authorities. And the reason was the fact that the civilians did not assist the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Assist the army in doing what?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In providing them with materiel and equipment and supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was happening in that municipality in terms of combat; was it a front line, was it a defensive area? What was it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kalesija was a so-called border-line municipality. During the war, i.e., after the end of the war, it became part of the Federation. During the war for a certain period of time it was in our hands. We can see here that the president of the municipality complained of something that was a commonplace occurrence along the border of Republika Srpska. Those Serbs in Podrinje and in Semberija had a reserve homeland, as it were. As I already told you, if people heard shots 20 kilometres away, the Serbs immediately fled across the Drina into Serbia. He provides a percentage here which is not realistic. He says that 70 per cent of the Serbs, i.e., our people, are in trenches, but that's 70 per cent of those who stayed behind in Kalesija. We have to take into account that 80 per cent had already fled. He doesn't criticise anybody. He just complains and he just -- he is fishing for sympathy. He wants people to understand that he is in dire straits. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was this a Serbian-dominated municipality, or what was the ethnic makeup before the war? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the ethnic structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole but not of individual municipalities. It's obvious that here Serbs were in the minority, a very small minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were Serbs from that municipality eventually expelled?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at what this president of municipality says, it seems they were not expelled, that they fled. They left the municipality themselves, because he mentions genocide here, but they were not physically driven out by the Muslims. They ran for their lives, fearing for their existence, their property, their survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's just go back quickly to page 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the problems you earlier had, finding what in the Supreme Defence Council minutes was found in page 18 and 19, you find it in 22 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's just go back -- oh, we are on the page that I'm interested in. Page 40, English and B/C/S, 40 at the top of the page, J000-1181.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You'll see this is an entry, Bijeljina, 15th of September, 1992. It's the same conference that we've been looking at in the Eastern Bosnian Corps. And we see there number 2 Special Brigade Ljubica Savic referred to - that's Mauzer, isn't it, Mr. Milovanovic? - and does that entry accord with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 2 I see here the 2nd Posavina Brigade commanded by Milad Berenja [phoen]. I don't see Ljubisa Savic Mauzer. I'm looking at page 41 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You should be on page 40 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's still 41. I see "Ljubisa Savic" in the English version, but I don't understand the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go to the place where the numbers usually are written up to the top, or do we have the whole of the page now? So apparently this is one. Yes, this is the right one. Let's proceed. It's a different one from what we had a minute ago. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to avoid confusion, Mr. Jordash is recorded as saying that he's working with page 1181, and I see 1170 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's J000-1170.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You can see the entry there. It seems as though the commander of the Eastern Bosnian Corps is reporting concerning Special Brigade Ljubisa Savic. And my question was: That Ljubisa Savic is or was Mauzer, and do the details there about his subordination and activities accord with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Mauzer. It's about that brigade that I spoke about yesterday, the Panthers or the Guards, as they call themselves. That brigade was not established by Ljubisa Savic but by Major Pantelic, and that's probably where the name Panthers comes from, from Pantelic. And that's how the fighting men were named. It's a small unit that were set up before the VRS. It's only 420 men, so it's not even a battalion, but they call themselves a brigade to seek popularity. And it says that from the beginning of the war he said -- it says they had 80 wounded and 20 dead. And that brigade commander was later succeeded by Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's return now to the Supreme Defence Council minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 1D3595. Page 20 -- sorry, page 18 of the English and 22 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm interested in what Pavle Bulatovic, federal minister of the interior, has to say concerning Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move, in English, to the next page because I finished those two lines by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please indicate when you finish the page, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just finished reading this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And read down to where Pavle Bulatovic picks up on what Zivota Panic has said.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've reached the reference to Momir Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as we can see from this entry, there's obviously a discussion about Ivanovic. And it appears that Bulatovic is essentially accusing the army, Panic, of arming Ivanovic from the Fourth of July Barracks and he's making that allegation on the basis that Ivanovic had been, it seems, reported to have said he had been equipped in the Fourth of July Barracks. Are you able to explain just very briefly your understanding of the Fourth of July Barracks, what it was at this point in time, August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The action is taking place in the territory of Serbia, Montenegro, and Kosovo. Republika Srpska has nothing to do with it. It's their mutual settlement of accounts and accusations. Bulatovic it blaming the Army of Yugoslavia that they had equipped this group and Panic is denying it. So I can't play referee here. I don't know whether it's accurate or not. I don't know this man Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to play referee. I'm asking you to explain what the Fourth of July Barracks was as far as you're aware. If you don't know, you don't know; but if you can assist, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Fourth of July Barracks is located in Belgrade. It housed mostly guards units from the garrison in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What is a guard unit?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guard units in every army, and also in the Army of Yugoslavia, are units that provide direct security to the Supreme Command, to the president of the state, the General Staff. They're also parade units used to -- for welcome ceremonies to foreign heads of state, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as seems to be suggested by Bulatovic, the Fourth July Barracks contained logistics and weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every barracks where there are soldiers and COs and officers have certain depots where equipment is stored, clothing, footwear, weapons, some ammunition, and Bulatovic is probably referring to the fact that those 1150 men in total were probably equipped from that depot, from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to 65 ter 5596.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, this is a Mladic notebook from November 1991 and it may be that you cannot comment, but I'm going to give it a try.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we have page -- page 362 of the English, 363 of the B/C/S, and 362 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I wanted to see if you can -- this helps to clarify issues relating to the Fourth of July Barracks. It's a Mladic entry, J000-2740, and at the top of the page of the English, and I'm interested in the section which begins: "Vuksan Milovic from the staff of the Serbian Guard in Belgrade received approval of Lieutenant-General Simovic that they got the Fourth of July Barracks in Belgrade, Backa Palanka, Novi Sad. The Guard will go there for training. They are preparing 2.500 men who will join us there -- join us here. The Guards Staff will include 10 people - officers which they will select - and 10 from the Serbian Republican Staff of the TO. I will be in contact with Major-General Vukovic." And do you know anything about this, the arming and training of the Serbian Guard force at the Fourth of July Barracks in Belgrade in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the clarity of the record, J000-2740 is P2929 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about this. At that time I was an operative officer at the command in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You do know who the Serbian Guard were though, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know what I saw on TV, like any other citizen, that some paramilitary units were coming into existence. I was engaged at that time as an operative in charge of Kosovo and Macedonia, and I know that some sort of paramilitary appeared at Skopska Gora in Macedonia, but I believe they left very soon afterwards and they were not, I believe, related to the Fourth of July Barracks. It was some sort of popular party from Sremska Mitrovica ran by some man Jovic who had formed six detachments bearing some traditional Serbian name such as Sindjelic. They tried to penetrate into Macedonia. But I simply don't know anything about the Fourth of July Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Let's move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just have a moment. Can we go back, please, to 65 ter 50-- sorry, 5063. And page 253 of the English, 247 of the B/C/S, and 246 at the top -- at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested in the entry which begins -- sorry, you don't have yours yet, but as that's coming up, I'm interested in the entry that begins: "Samac, 7th of December, 1992, Monday, 950 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we go over the page with the English to page 254 of the English and 248, I think, of the B/C/S, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we're talking about a meeting with the leadership of the Samac municipality. And Dr. Simic, president of the municipality, is present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we can move to page 256 of the English and 249 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are we there, Mr. Milovanovic, in the original, where it begins: "Stevan Todorovic, SJB chief"?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have page 249, the meeting with representatives from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There isn't a number on the top of the page, that might be what's difficult. But it should be, I think, 248. Or strangely on my copy it's between 247 and 248.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm looking at 231.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist, the record is saying 5063 and I have found it under 65 ter 5603. That could be the cause of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, my mistake. I beg your pardon, 5603. I do apologise to Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 5603, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I suggest that you move on to a page which is known to you. And would you please take care that your apologies only will not already take a considerable time in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure I did anything wrong there. I gave the numbers that I had, which are the right numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what's then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the B/C/S original page number is, but I've given what the indication I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have to take care that you know the English page numbers and the B/C/S page numbers. It's always possible -- if they're okay now, then of course there's no problem. But it could well be, let me have a look ... Is there any way that "Stevan Todorovic" appears at the very end of this page, chief of the SJB? At least it looks, more or less. And also the date of the 18th of April, 1992, seems to be corresponding. I'm -- it's your exhibit, it's your witness, but that seems to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But that's the page numbers I've given, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So that's correct now. So then put your question. We have now -- at least I have a English page and a B/C/S page which are corresponding. So why not ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you read the entry "Stevan Todorovic," please, Mr. Milovanovic. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm putting my question as soon as I can, so please read that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is, of course, half an entry because it stops in the middle of a line. I don't know whether you want us, whether in B/C/S or in English, to read the whole of that line, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'd like him to read the entry, I'd like everyone to read the entry, then we'll go over the page to finish off that entry, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you there, Mr. Milovanovic? We can then move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read the entire page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just for the avoidance of doubt, I'm interested in what Todorovic is saying about the sending of men to Ilok for training and what happens to them subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we now also, for the benefit of witness, enlarge the top portion of the left page. A little bit more perhaps. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For the record: J000-4672.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've come up to the 19th of May and Colonel Stevan Nikolic who says that he has to go to Belgrade, which means that I've read everything concerning Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you know about these men being sent by Colonel Jeremic and General Bulic to Ilok for training?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. That was in April 1992 when I was still in Nis. And I can see here the name Todorovic. I knew him, I spoke to him several times on the phone. Stevan Todorovic had two nicknames, Steve and Crni. Here he only brags that he sent some people for training in Ilok, in Srem, which means that he sent them outside of the Republika Srpska territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of a special battalion that had been formed under the command of Crni and then subordinated to Colonel Nikolic in operations in Sanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you know a Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my information, Mr. Milovanovic, in the portion we just read we see that Dragan Djordjevic is -- has as a nickname or is also known as Crni, and the same would be true for Todorovic, they would both have the same nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On that subject, could we please go to 65 ter 5600, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And page 377 at the top, please. And you see the entry there - this is J000-3551 - the entry which begins with: "Divjak, his nickname is Crni, there are six of them with the same nickname, three are stealing in order to discredit me." Was Crni a common name? Is it a common name? Or was it a common nickname, I should say, during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people were self-styled Crni. That's the nickname six of them adopted, because Crni amongst Serbs is a synonym for something terrible and terrifying. And the Crni that we spoke about yesterday was from Belica. He moved from Herzegovina. Wherever there were problems amongst civilian authorities, where it was easy to loot and amass riches, he appeared there. He got in touch with those who were of the same problematic behaviour. As I was reading this, I found the materials in the notebook, and in brackets there is the name and the family name of that Crni from Belica. That's the same man who had been in Mladic's office and Mladic sent him to me. Everything that he was saying was aimed at preventing his detention, because he had killed a man, but his story was that he had killed that man in order to protect the corps commander or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, before we go through the details of the behaviour of every Crni in the former Yugoslavia, I do understand that Crni was a nickname which was used with some frequency and referred to something terrible. That's, I think, was the question, isn't it, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That question has been answered. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to return to something we touched on yesterday, Mr. Milovanovic, because I think it's fair to give you an opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have P386 on the screen, please. This is the combat readiness and activities of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992 analysis, dated April 1993. And I'm interested in page 61 of the English and 55 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as we can see we're dealing with a section of the report which is looking back at the training within -- training and education within the VRS. And I think we can start off with - if you could find in the text - "The Main Problems That Arose Were," then we can lead off from there.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read about the main problems that arose in training.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you see the section --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps we need to go to B/C/S page 56 and English 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- where it says: "After these initial problems which occurred in most of our units, the consequences of which were a large number of killed and wounded officers and men in the unit, measures were taken in most units to improve training and retrain the men and the officers."?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let's just go to one more reference, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 64 of the English and B/C/S page 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's under C, "The Training of Critical Skills," and you'll see, in the English at least, it's about seven or more like ten lines down, where it says: "Lack of training is the main reason for the large number of dead and wounded." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So do you accept -- do you accept that training was problematic and did lead -- the lack of training did lead to an increased number of dead and wounded in 1992 at least?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a three-and-a-half-year long war experience, which tells me that out of the number of dead 80 per cent were due to a human mistake. I don't want to teach you about the international standards of human losses, which is 8 per cent by the way. The Army of Republika Srpska suffered total losses of between 7 and 8 per cent. And when I said that 80 per cent of men are killed due to human mistake, I primarily meant a lack of training. An officer cannot help a soldier to shelter, to target well, to shoot well. On the previous page we could read how people were recruited into the JNA. They were of different ethnic groups. Serbs were mostly recruited as infantry men, as quartermasters, men as drivers. When the war started, we had artillery tanks, aeroplanes, all sorts of things, and we had to retrain our -- those infantry men for various specialties. One of the main causes of loss in the Army of Republika Srpska was the lack of training. The time was really short. As I told you yesterday, the first eight months of training meant that we did not use young recruits in combat. However, we inherited a large contingent of military conscripts aged between 23, which is the age when they were no longer under the obligation to serve in the army, until the age of 55. When they served in the army, they were trained on obsolete weapons. In the meantime the weapons were modernised and they didn't know how to use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, is there a lot of dispute about that; if people are badly trained and the circumstances may not have allowed for such perfect training, that this would have a negative impact on casualties and wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the document apparently says that this was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I was just getting to the real point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get to the real point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we go to page 61 of the B/C/S and 68 of the English, there's a section there which deals with final recommendations concerning what should happen in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the first entry concerning what should be done is that the Main Staff of the RS and the air force and the anti-aircraft defence must devote greater attention to material training resources and teaching aids, and the first entry is: "The maintenance and guarding of training-grounds, drill grounds, and durable and expendable teaching supplies." Now, my question is -- do you have that, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My question is - and it's not a criticism, it's just a question: Why was it that the VRS didn't open more training-grounds to deal with this deficit?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have money. We used the training-grounds in Manjaca and Kalinovik that we inherited from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you didn't call on assistance from Serbia, from the FRY, to assist you with training?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The FRY accepted to train officers and non-commissioned officers following the regular peacetime curriculum, which means that their training lasted for four years. That's why we had to establish our own training centres to train our own officers and non-commissioned officers in the duration of six months and one year respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So apart from this assistance in training officers and non-commissioned officer, you, the VRS, did not receive assistance from the FRY in terms of training recruits or non-officers; is that right, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not ask for that kind of assistance because the FRY was not supposed to be involved in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the first place. We did not want the FRY to be a warring party in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the same way the Republic of Croatia was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just -- we'll come back to this shortly, but it was noted - and we can turn to it if we need to - in this combat report that there was good -- your assessment, the VRS assessment in April of 1993 was that in 1992 there had been good co-operation between the military intelligence services but in terms of co-operation between the VRS intelligence service and the Serbian MUP intelligence service, that co-operation was unsatisfactory in 1992; can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question, especially within the MUP context. What MUP did you have in mind? Who did not co-operate with whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. I can find the exact piece of text I'm looking for in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we take a break first. But could I seek some clarification of one of the last answers. You said, Mr. Milovanovic: "The FRY accepted to train officers and non-commissioned officers following the regular peacetime curriculum, which means that their training lasted for four years." Does this mean that this offer could not be accepted because it would have taken too much time anyhow to have them trained in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We accepted the offer and we did sends our candidates for officers and non-commissioned officers for training, but we had to wait for them to come back. The war had to stop, and we were sure that we would win and that the VRS would continue functioning and we would certainly benefit from those officers. But we couldn't wait for the cycle to be over. We lost 17.400 men in combat. 38 per cent, 6.600 of them, were officers and non-commissioned officers. I'm again repeating that the world norm is 8 per cent losses of the overall loss and we suffered 38 per cent losses among our officer staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it was reasonable or not reasonable what you did and whether you had good reasons to do so is a different matter. I just asked on whether it was -- the offer was accepted. I do, therefore, understand that part of those to be trained as officers and non-commissioned officers were not available because they were being trained by the FRY. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. And we resume at ten minutes to 11.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue: Mr. Jordash, you received instructions from the Registry what you should provide in order to be sure that the documents you would like to have on the screen would be on the screen. Now, I do understand that you say you can't do that and that you're referring to page numbers at the top of the page handwritten. Let's make one thing perfectly clear. Whatever is handwritten in a document or typed in a document or whatever is content of the document. For a document to be on the screen, you can't start searching in the content of a document. You need the e-court pages, references, what is the document, what are the ... Now, I do understand that although the Registry has again tried again and again to assist you in this matter, if you say, "I can't give you those references," you are missing an opportunity to put a document to a witness. It's not just a matter of saying, "We need in this document, which is 300 pages, we need a page which at the top there's a handwritten reference of ..." especially if they are not in sequential order. So the Registry will still try to assist you, but if you don't come up with the e-court data needed in order to call them on the screen, the consequence simply is that you don't have the document there to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The problem is that I didn't want to and didn't plan to work from the original. That was Mr. Groome's idea. That idea was adopted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- by the Chamber yesterday. We finished court at 7.00. With the best will in the world we couldn't go through the whole of the diaries and find the page numbers overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say, I could do that -- again, Mr. Jordash, you're explaining to me what is problematic. What you should do is to say, "I could solve the problem if you would allow me to go back to the non-handwritten originals, but only to the B/C/S version," then we would consider that and we would avoid the chaos. I think, as a matter of fact, that there was never a ruling of the Chamber on that. What we suggested was to have them both on the screen so that -- and that was a suggestion. That was not an order. If you would have said, "But this causes us problems, in giving the Registry the right information to get them on the screen," we would have considered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But yesterday there didn't seem to be a problem, so I didn't think about this overnight because we didn't seem to have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we had problems today. And I do agree with you that yesterday, where the Registry did it's utmost best to assist you, that -- and they're still willing to do that, but if we end up -- and let's not forget that this morning we had a problem which was just bad preparation. If you do not know that the B/C/S is found on page 22 and we start looking through page 18 and 19 for three or four minutes, that's, of course, a waste of time. And that's a matter that in a well organised preparation of the Defence should have been dealt with. And it's not the first. And, again, I'm not going to -- I'm really solution oriented, but the only thing I want to say is that if you want a document on the screen and if you say -- and I should not talk too quickly. If you say, "I can do it but unfortunately not on the handwritten ones," then you could have gone to Mr. Groome, you could have told him that until now at no point in time reference was made to asterisks or to specific matters in the handwriting. We all, if we wish to, can have the originals on our screen. The only thing is then that the witness doesn't see it. But any party seeing any particulars on the handwritten version - and you have your computers available to follow it, and Mr. Groome also has - then can say, "I would like this page now to be shown, it's found on e-court page 256." Let's try to always find ways to resolve existing problems. Mr. Groome, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just two thing briefly, Your Honour. If it would avoid confusion, I think it may be enough just to inform General Milovanovic that any time he wishes to see the original, if that would assist him, that's available. And secondly, the Prosecution has been preparing a table which I will tender tomorrow which is simply the reference, the J number, the transcript page reference number, and hopefully the Chamber will admit that and that should allow at least a clear record of what specific entries have been discussed in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, that's what we need on the record. But our first concern was how to get documents on the screen the Defence wishes to have on the screen. Mr. Jordash, has the guidance been sufficient? If you say alternative ways will avoid a waste of time, then we would seriously consider to proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the page numbers I have, and I'm now confused, the page numbers I have are the ones which I've been indicating, which are the B/C/S and the English and the top of the page. They're the only page numbers I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but there --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- and there's nothing I can do to rectify that at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you had prepared, before, isn't it? Before the witness came.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, with those page numbers, the ones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The handwritten page numbers at the top of the pages? Mr. Jordash, we need e-court numbers. And if they are the same, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I've been saying the e-court numbers for the typed copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. For the typed copies. And there, apparently, seems to be the problem, that Mr. Groome had suggested to use the handwritten version, and that now apparently causes the problems in calling the documents on the screen. And if this resolves it, then I think Mr. Groome already said, Okay, let's then, if that resolves the problem, Mr. Milovanovic is hereby informed that whenever he would like to look at the handwritten version, that it is available but that we start working from the transcribed original. Now, Mr. Jordash, from now on, if you are talking about the B/C/S, you are talking about the B/C/S typewritten transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's that version of the original. Madam Registrar, does that give sufficient guidance if you get the e-court numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Not exactly. I would need the number of the document among three or five documents that are uploaded under the same 65 ter number. So which two documents are you using and which pages on each document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So if I give the ERN number, does that assist?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For example, doc ID. So, yeah. Doc ID for -- you give me first 65 ter number, I open the document, there are five documents uploaded under this number. So I need, for B/C/S, this doc ID; English, this doc ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that for Madam Registrar part of the problem is that documents are uploaded, are re-uploaded, sometimes are already admitted into evidence, so therefore that ... but, let's get started and let's see whether it works. And if not, Mr. Jordash, you're invited to discuss the matter with Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you were witnessing, as a witness, a procedural discussion which we hope to leave behind us at this moment. Mr. Jordash will now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's return to P386, which is the combat readiness and activities of the Army of the RS in 1992. And, please, could we have on the screen page 83 of the English and 74 of the B/C/S. And we are looking at the section dealing with intelligence and security support. And this part is 5.1, intelligence support. And if we can then turn to page 85 of the English and 76 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the paragraph I'm interested in begins: "Co-operation and exchange of data with related services in the territory of RS is generally satisfactory, as well as with the Main Staff of the SVRSK. Of late, co-operation has also been intensified with the intelligence and security organs of the Army of Yugoslavia, while with the Ministry of the Interior, the Republic of Serbia, it is still at an unsatisfactory level."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then if we can move, for completeness, to page 90 of the English and 80 of the B/C/S, dealing with security as opposed to intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 10: "Co-operation with related services in the territories of the RS, the RSK and the FR Yugoslavia grew in proportion to the development of the intelligence security system of the Army of RS and the MUP of RS. We consider the co-operation with related services in the Serbian army, the RS Krajina, and the National Security Service of Republika Srpska until now to have been very good, professional, and untrammelled by any subjective obstacles. Our co-operation with the MUP of Republika Srpska and especially with the MUP of the Republic of Serbia and of the FR Yugoslavia we consider to have been unsatisfactory. The main cause being, in our opinion, the passivity of the organs mentioned and their reluctance to expand co-operation with us." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is that your view? Was that your view?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The analysis of combat readiness was prepared in seven segments. The one we looked at before was training and education, that's my segment as Chief of Staff. This security and intelligence segment was prepared by the security and intelligence sector, that is General Tolimir. I see here two problems that Tolimir pointed out in this analysis. The first problem is the mutual co-operation of intelligence services in the environment. Under the law, intelligence services of friendly countries are required to co-operate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, the first question is - I do now understand that this part was not authored by you or not prepared by you: Is your view different from the one which is written down here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position is consistent with what is written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That answers the question, I take it, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was this lack of co-operation a discussion amongst the Main Staff and the meetings that were held amongst the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before the analysis we read the whole analysis together and that was an opportunity for people to make remarks to others, if they had any.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But had General Tolimir raised this issue prior to the compilation of this report during a Main Staff meeting? Had he come, for example, and said, this is the issue, I'm reporting to you, reporting to Mladic, this is the situation with the problems of co-operation with the Serbian intelligence, civil intelligence service, the DB?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a continuous topic. And this is an analysis of the annual performance of the VRS citing both good and bad things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was there any indication during these discussions or at the time this report was compiled which touched upon the reasons why the Serbian DB was passive in relation to anticipated or hoped-for co-operation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about co-operation with the Ministry of the Interior, not with the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the Ministry of the Interior's intelligence service was the State Security of Serbia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I'm not so conversant with the structure of security in Serbia. But our intelligence service was required to co-operate with our Ministry of the Interior, that means the MUP of Republika Srpska. The army was not required to co-operate with the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We were required to co-operate with the intelligence service of the General Staff of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. In terms of co-operation with the Serbian MUP in relation to other issues other than intelligence issues, was that a discussion at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was discussed and Tolimir was always directed to co-operate with the MUP of Serbia and to have this co-operation through the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, we're talking about this combat readiness report dated April of 1993. Am I correct that Stanisic was not a subject for discussion at the Main Staff, Stanisic's co-operation with the VRS, for example? That wasn't something that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my last testimony I was directed by the president of the Trial Chamber to study 54 reports by Tolimir, intelligence briefs that he prepared and sent to various addresses. And he regularly wrote to them that he sent them also to Jovica Stanisic, which he was not required to do; and to me, although we were only two metres away from each other; General Djukic, the minister - can somebody help me? it was not Sokolovic at the time, it was somebody else - the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia, which he didn't have to do. And I also wrote a manuscript to the Trial Chamber explaining that Tolimir was doing that irregularly and unlawfully, aiming to present himself as co-operating with various institutions in the Balkans. His name -- Stanisic's name was used irregularly, and I'm apologizing to him now that he was involved in something where he didn't belong. Tolimir just put him of his own accord on his mailing list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether Mr. Stanisic, and Mr. Stanisic's co-operation with the VRS, whether that was something discussed at meetings of the Main Staff. That was the question. Was it or was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was never any discussion about Jovica Stanisic as chief of the State Security of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stanisic first appears in the diary -- sorry, in the notebooks on the 2nd of July, 1993. So he doesn't appear in 1991 and he doesn't appear in 1992, and neither is he mentioned. Does that surprise you, from your interaction with Mladic, your conversations with him, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not surprise me. I don't know in what context Jovica appeared on the 2nd of July, 1992. I know that my first contact with him was on the 22nd or 23rd January, 1993, at Mount Tara in the Panorama Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, just to be clear: He appears in the diary for the first time on the 2nd of July, 1993. And just so you understand the situation, his telephone number doesn't appear in the diaries from 1991 to 1995, the notebooks. Does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mladic's notes. Which contain, for your information, tens and tens and tens of other telephone numbers.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've got me confused now. In my last testimony, between two breaks we discussed some meeting recorded in Mladic's diary, a meeting in Slavonia, and the dilemma was whether Mladic is -- Mladic was talking to Stanisic or he was writing down what Stanisic was saying at that meeting, and we concluded in the end that Mladic was writing down Stanisic's words. Because what was written there was that Stanisic had informed the meeting that he had sent some eight men to Tenja. Tenja being a place in Slavonia. So I don't think it's a correct version that Stanisic's name was not mentioned in 1991 and 1992. And you also added throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I think you've misunderstood the point I was making or asking you about. What I was suggesting was that Stanisic's telephone number doesn't appear in the notebooks and I was asking you whether that is a surprise to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, isn't it true that you asked two questions? The first whether it was a surprise that Mr. Stanisic appears only in the 2nd of July, 1993, and the second is whether it's a surprise that the telephone number of Mr. Stanisic ... So I think the witness commented on the first question. And then to say that he didn't understand the question, because you put both questions to him, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I didn't put both questions. I confirmed and corrected the witness's understanding about the 2nd of July, 1992, and then I moved on to the second question. But if it was confusing, then I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then it's unclear to me what the answer is to the first question. But if you move on, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to the 2nd of July, 1993, meeting which Mr. Stanisic attended. Before we do that, though, let me ask you something. At any point in time are you aware of any centre established by the MUP of Serbia in Pale in 1993 or 1994 or 1995, a centre for supplies?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the same question in relation to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of Herzegovina either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know a place called Talic in Bosnia, which was within, or might have been within, VRS territory?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the last name Talic, such as General Momir Talic, but I'm not aware of that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. So it follows that you're not aware of any centre for supplies in any place called Talic, which, I am in agreement with you, we've not been able to find it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's turn to -- let's go to P5 -- sorry, P2529. English page 1, B/C/S page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is the meeting Mr. Stanisic attended, and agrees he attended, on 2nd of July, 1993. Just take a moment to read this.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it up to number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Keep going then until we get to what Stanisic is alleged to have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps on the English we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need it in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Next page then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see Stanisic's name on this page. I see Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Go one more page then in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now see Stanisic's name after Sainovic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it should say: "The majority of what we need should be issued by the MUP of Serbia. The centres should be Pale, Herzegovina, and Talic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are now two pages ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When the witness said he didn't see any page, we had moved to the third page of this document, and there he doesn't appear, and then the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I have the B/C/S pages in the typed copy but not in this handwritten. Apparently they are the same though.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now see the first page. "The majority of what we need should be issued via the MUP of Serbia. The centres should be Pale, Herzegovina, and Talic."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Does that make any sense whatsoever to you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't make any sense. I told you that I don't know anything about the existence of this centre at Pale, Herzegovina. I also don't know that man Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we're in agreement on that issue. The meeting begins, as we can see, with President Sainovic introducing -- or somebody, probably Sainovic, introducing Badza and Stanisic and Sainovic as the men who carry out things. Does it follow from what you've said so far in your testimony that from your military experience in 1992 up until this point Stanisic wasn't, for you, a man who carried out things for the VRS or played a role in the military operations that you were conducting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, we see there at page 3 of the English and 3 of the B/C/S that Mladic takes Sainovic's telephone number but he doesn't appear to take Stanisic's or Badza's. Were you aware that Mladic had taken a number and then was in touch with Sainovic directly from this point onwards, or is that not something you can testify to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I never read Mladic's notes unless he himself opened the notebook and read to me something that I, according to him, needed to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we then read towards the end of this entry, there is a discussion, it seems, about a group called the Black Hand and Lukic. Could you confirm that in July of 1993 there was a good deal of governmental concern from Serbia about the behaviour of Lukic and that concern led to demands to the VRS, to Mladic, to arrest him and have him dealt with? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't because I learned of Lukic and the Black Hand only when the indictment was issued against Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's go to the next meeting Stanisic is present at, on the 8th of July, 1993, meeting with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's P2530. And if you would turn to page -- can we turn, please, to page 5 of the English and 5 of the B/C/S, where Stanisic is said to be speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Stanisic is said to say: "Our assessments have not been checked thoroughly, some might be angered. Our assessment about the situation and the VRS and the RS are not as they should be in view of our position. Some commanders can jeopardise the system in Serbia - some can act as paramilitaries." Are you able to confirm that at this point in time Stanisic was complaining about men who were subordinated to the VRS in Bosnia returning to Serbia and acting as paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm this because I did not attend that meeting. I only realised all that here in the courtroom as I'm reading notes in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 6 of -- no, let's go to page 5 -- let's stay with page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just if we could look at the original and see if you are able to say anything about whether the comment under "Weaknesses" can be attributed to Stanisic according to any indication you can see on the document, i.e., are there any signs which enable you to say that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No comment. I only saw the text yesterday evening and I'm looking at it now again. I underline that I did not attend that meeting, so I am in no position to know what the atmosphere was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page because there's a particular point I'm interested in having you have a look at. Stanisic is said to have said, or perhaps that might be one inference from this document: "That we, from Serbia, take over the financing of the MUP as well. That, with the assistance of the police, we helped Generals Mladic and Novakovic achieve goals." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps you know, perhaps you don't; are you able to confirm that the Serbian MUP did not, as this comment suggests, finance the Bosnian Serb MUP?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia financed about seven and a half thousand of officers of the Army of Republika Srpska and it committed to finance 50.000 soldiers. The latter never came through. I don't know that the MUP of Serbia financed the MUP of Republika Srpska. I personally don't think that that was the case, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you think that wasn't the case?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know what hardships the MUP of Republika Srpska had to go through. They were as poor as the army. This is not Stanisic's decision. This is just a proposal that we from Serbia should take over the financing of both MUP organisations in order to help Mladic and Novakovic. Mladic and Novakovic were army commanders of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbia Krajina respectively. What Mr. Stanisic meant when he said that the financing of the MUP should be of assistance to the militaries, I don't know. Maybe he just sought ways to relieve the government budget in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's turn to the 14th of December, 1993. And it's P2532. Page 7 of the English and B/C/S. And this is the fourth -- or I should say, it's the continuation of the fourth meeting that Stanisic attended. And there's a mistake apparently in e-court. The English has an extra page. The last page in English is not there for the B/C/S in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before we turn to the portion I'm interested in, did you know a man called Karasic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. We were at school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Wasn't Karasic -- the Karasic that I'm interested in was a police officer. No? Did you know somebody called Karasic who was a member of the Bosnian Serb MUP? Karisic [phoen]. Subordinated to Stupar during operation Pancir-2. That might help.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the name of Karasic on this page. All I see is the name of Krajisnik towards the bottom of the page. This may be a mistake in translation. I attended that meeting. I don't remember that Karasic attended it, and I know Karasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, so who was Karasic then? Was he subordinated to Stupar during Operation Pancir-2?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not have been subordinated to Stupar. Karasic was in the Republika Srpska MUP and he was responsible for those two brigades or Special Police Units or combat units of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, on several occasions we have the name "Karasic" on the record, whereas the witness is actually talking about a person named "Karisik." I believe that this is what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You want this to be verified. The person you were describing, could you spell his last name. That's the person responsible for the -- those two brigades or Special Police Units, could you spell his last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] K-a-r-i-s-i-k. I believe that his name was Milenko, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you know a person by the name Karasic? And I'll spell that for you, K-a-r-a-s-i-c.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The man in the Republika Srpska MUP responsible for the two brigades or Special Police Units, who was he subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was subordinated to the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who it was at that time. Mico Stanisic held that office twice and I think that that was his second time in office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at this meeting on the 14th of December, 1993. Can we go -- you're present, it seems; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document says 13th. Or is that a mistake, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think the excerpt contained both the 13th and the 14th, and the one I'm looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- says the 14th, on the English at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That meeting started on the 13th and ended on the 14th, which means that we continued working on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we go to page 8 in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that this was a meeting which had been called by Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired by Milosevic but the meeting was actually called by Karadzic. You can see that on the 13th Karadzic was the first speaker. He was the one who opened the meeting, and not Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think if we go back to the 13th of December --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 1 of the English and 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- we'll see that Stanisic apparently opens the meeting. He doesn't say anything else during -- well, he says one other thing apparently, but he introduces the topic of the meeting. Do you recall that or not?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held in the state security building which is why Stanisic opened the meeting, as the host, the head of that institution. And Karadzic's was actually the keynote address.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to page 8 of the English and 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And according to the note Stanisic is supposed to have offered to spare 120 men and Karisik. Does that make any sense to you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not. Stanisic could not offer Karisik to us because Karisik was ours. Maybe he meant that he could place the 120 men under Karisik's command. He says, We can spare 100 to 120 men and Karisik. I suppose that what he had in mind were Karisik's Special Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It seems to me that in the document itself there is a problem with translation. It says we can spare 100 to 100 [as interpreted] men together with Karisik. I believe that the English translation does not reflect the original as well as it should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll have to check, first of all, from what it is translated into English, is it from the original handwritten version or is it from the transcribed version in B/C/S. Apparently a matter to be verified. If the parties could agree on there possibly being a mistake and agree on what it should be, then they are invited to report this to the Chamber. If not, we'll have to ask a report from CLSS. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection of Stanisic speaking at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I already stated that during my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I've missed that. Do you -- you recall him introducing the meeting; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't. That was my first arrival in Belgrade. I must have been a bit confused. I really didn't understand why I was invited to that meeting at all in view of the fact that the commander was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall him saying anything concerning Karisik or the contents of what is written there underneath his name?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember because the previous page reflects my discussion. Because Karadzic wanted us to be on our own around Sarajevo. Actually, that's what I wanted. I wanted us to act independently around Sarajevo. I didn't want to -- the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to meddle. And I hoped that everybody would accept my proposal; however, Jovica said what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the MUP of Serbia can spare 100 to 120 men together with Karisik. And I would add to that: that he probably meant together with Karisik's specials or his special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that never materialised. Instead of Stanisic's 100 to 120 men, the same number arrived from the 72nd Brigade of the corps of Special Forces of the Army of Yugoslavia. And this happened unbeknownst to me or General Mladic. Colonel Stupar took them directly to the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. They were defeated, and then on the 28th of December I sent them packing. And I returned then to Belgrade. They had had 13 dead, about 40 wounded, and 4 men had gone missing and I don't think that they were ever found.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm reminded that these men from the 72nd Brigade wore red berets and were known by that item; is that right? Mr. Milovanovic, are you there? The red -- the 72nd Brigade under Stupar, were they known for wearing red berets? And were they known by some as the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's two questions. If we could separate those out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
