utterances.text: Let's deal with the first question, Mr. Milovanovic. Did they wear red berets?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day after they suffered the disaster I found them sporting red berets in front of the Park Hotel in Vogosca. Actually, they were not wearing red berets, they had them in their back-packs. Yesterday we spoke about the Red Berets and I told you that the only person I saw wearing a red beret was Mr. Frenki. However, when we spoke about the Red Berets yesterday, we were talking about the police and not about the military. In conclusion, I would like to say that the soldiers from the 72nd Brigade did indeed have red berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You've mentioned a few times about the fact that you don't know any other Red Berets other than having seen Frenki, I think, in 1993. Did you know somebody called Nenad Kajkut?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me have on the screen 1D05283. May we have a break, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break, but I would like to deal with the procedural matter for which we -- that's about bar table matters, which I'd rather do at the end of this portion. There's no need for the accused to be present. If you insist on your presence, Mr. Stanisic, then of course we would do it immediately after the break, but otherwise we could shorten the break slightly. So if you -- we'll ask the witness, any way, to already to leave the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in approximately a half an hour, Mr. Milovanovic, because we'll deal with a procedural matter with which we'll not bother you. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- I would like to deal with a very technical matter on bar table documents. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Stanisic, if he prefers to leave already, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, if he could, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the same is true for Mr. Simatovic, but we'll have a follow-up discussion, very briefly, on the bar table submissions the Chamber is expecting. You are free to leave as you wish, to do so. And if you insist to be present, then, of course, we would do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the matter I would like to raise with you is the bar table motions which are expected to be filed. And I'm not, at this moment, discussing the dead-lines. The Chamber is worried about the numbers you've indicated for the first one, I think 600 documents; for the second one, 200 documents; and a third one yet unspecified. The purpose of tendering documents through bar table submissions is to give further details on well-known matters - let's keep it short - to say that where a document is easily introduced without a witness who can explain about the document. Now, what is worrying us is that, that numbers where bar table documents, exhibits, are expected to add something to well-known issues, or -- that it would -- 600 plus 200 would by far double the whole body of documentary evidence we have received until now by the -- during the Defence case. I'm not saying that the number in itself causes, as such, major problems, but the Chamber is a bit concerned. If, for example -- let me just give an example: If you say, "We want the Chamber to be aware of the operational combat activities between the 1st of July and the 1st of December of a certain year, and our main purpose is to establish that never Mr. Stanisic is mentioned," then that is a clear project where it's clear what the documentation is about. Of course, the next question would be, "If he never appears there, couldn't you agree on that with the other party, which saves us to go through a hundred or 150 or 200 documents?" The Chamber is not only worried about the numbers. Again, numbers in itself do not cause always problems. But where the descriptions are not yet clear whether -- where you are still working hard on it, the Chamber has some concern that finally we would end up with the leftovers of 65 ter lists, unspecified, unorganized, unstructured, and then finally it will be for the Chamber to find out what it is all about. Just to give you one example where it is -- where it was accepted. I think it was in the Gotovina case that the Defence had a specific interest in showing what had happened in the years before, atrocities committed by the Serbs, as background information. Now, if you then file ten or 15 or 20 or 30 or 40 or 50 reports describing that, then it's perfectly clear what the purpose of it is, why it is also not necessary to have them introduced by witnesses, but the numbers and the -- until now, and I emphasise that, the total lack of knowledge about structure, purpose, et cetera, causes quite some concerns to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I mean, well, if I've given that impression that I don't have an understanding of what is coming, then I apologise. I can be quite clear: The first report is going to be a continuation of the issue in relation -- sorry, the first bar table is going to be a continuation of the issue relating to DB activities dismantling paramilitaries. It will be clearly -- it will be clear to Your Honours what the documents -- we've made a selection of the documents. We haven't, by any means, put the majority into the bar table. We've made a selection which we felt gave Your Honours a clear picture of the size and magnitude of those activities. And included within that will be the reports which deal with such things as training by other entities to demonstrate the point that the DB was not involved in training. The second bar table, and this is where there might be room for new --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see. For example, if you say the -- and I just now first focus on the first category. DB activities dismantling paramilitaries. If there are -- I don't know how many documents there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think in the region of 300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. 300. Is there no way, if you have looked at that, to agree on that the DB has shown activities in this and this and this places to -- or at least that documentation exists indicating that the DB was engaged in dismantling paramilitary organisations there and there and there under the name so and so and so and so and so? Of course, the issue is not, I take it, the documents, but whether what was documented really happened and whether that was the only thing that happened. I take it that that is -- are usually the issues. Therefore, I'm really wondering whether we have to -- whether, if such documentation exists, whether it could not be summarised in perhaps four or five or six pages, saying, "Here, this, this, was reported by" and then that -- because the Chamber would also have to go through that in every single detail. What I would suggest to the parties is that where there is a lot of confusion about how to prepare, what to prepare, timing, et cetera, that you would meet together with Chamber staff and -- because we would very much like to digest and to go through that documentation before the judgement is rendered rather than after the judgement is rendered, and of course we need time for it as well. I suggest that the parties meet with Chamber staff to find out what is the most practical way in proceeding with apparently relevant documentation which the Stanisic Defence is seeking to have tendered -- to be tendered into evidence and to be admitted into evidence. Would that be a suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it's a suggestion, and of course I'll do exactly what Your Honours suggest. I wonder, though, whether, given the Prosecution's position as led through Mr. Theunens in large part, the DB's behaviour encouraged and intended to encourage the paramilitaries within Bosnia and Croatia, it's difficult to concede from our perspective too readily to any diminishing or summarising of evidence which demonstrates, in our view, the complete opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course I haven't seen that evidence so I can't comment on it in any way, but sometimes I'm aware that proving that A was done doesn't necessarily mean that B was not done, that doing A doesn't prevent you from doing B at the same time. I'm not saying it happened. But if you have a look at it and if the Prosecution would see all the documentation, I would say, yes, yes, there's clear documentation that efforts were made in that and that direction. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, and, I mean, we're not -- we obviously don't take the position that that -- what happened in Serbia demonstrates that nothing happened outside of Serbia. We obviously don't take that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, but, therefore, what you want to demonstrate is that activities existed and that documentation exists on those activities which tend in a different direction, in direction of dismantling paramilitary organisations. And then you could see whether it's limited to some or all known paramilitary organisations. Look at it and see whether you can find common ground which would allow you perhaps to diminish the number of documents to be -- to be bar tabled. Mr. Groome, you are on your feet as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I stood to say that the Prosecution would welcome an opportunity to discuss whether some of the facts that Mr. Jordash is seeking to establish with these documents could not be the subject of agreement. I stood up when he said the number 300 because I'm guessing - I haven't seen these document - that they're probably police reports and maybe judicial opinions about individual paramilitary groups. It seems to me that we -- it's likely that after having an opportunity to review all those police reports the Prosecution would agree that certain people were arrested on certain days and there was an ultimate disposition of their case, and that would, I think, end up in a one- or two-page chart, rather than 300 individual documents. And we're willing to undergo that process with Mr. Jordash. And I think in the end it would save all of us an awful lot of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I welcome any chance to diminish our work, so I'm happy to sit down with Mr. Groome and do as Your Honours suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you be assisted -- would you first sit together with Mr. Groome alone, coffee or tea, I leave it to you, and then with -- then to report to Chamber staff? Or would you prefer already to start with Chamber staff? And, again, when I say Chamber staff, that is in order for the Chamber not to be directly involved in evidentiary matters before they are before the Chamber. That's -- or make that the first point of your discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, but what might also be useful, I don't know if this is a useful suggestion, is if Your Honours have any particular concerns beyond the quantity, i.e., the issues, then that might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends. The quantity in itself doesn't worry me automatically. More important is whether there's a clear structure of what this documentation is establishing. And then if it's -- if that's clear on a factual basis - I'm not talking about any inferences to be made from that - then of course if there's documentary evidence, the first question is, Couldn't you agree on what the documentary evidence says without the Chamber staff going through every footnote or whatever in those 300 documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I mean, the -- I mean, I have to say, I mean, I completely agree that we can sit down and it can be useful, but I have to say, for the record, that the case led by Theunens was not pled on the indictment, it wasn't pled in the pre-trial brief, which means that we are somewhat trying to hit a constantly moving target. That's why we've gone large, because we don't know what the Prosecution intend to say about that and we don't know what Your Honours will find in relation to whether notice was sufficient or not, given the absence of whether it's cured in not being in the pre-trial brief and the indictment. So it might help if the Prosecution also indicated whether they intend to rely upon that belated allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that you meet on short notice and that to the extent you think it would be useful that you invite Chamber staff, that is, Mr. Nilsson, and perhaps it would even be better that you start a exchanging with Mr. Nilsson what the Chamber's concerns are, and then perhaps in a follow-up meeting, once you may have exchanged suggestions on how to meet those concerns and how to reduce the number of documents, to see whether you can make any progress. So I would suggest to start with Mr. Nilsson then perhaps to remove him and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say that I think from the Prosecution's point of view a meeting with Chamber staff would not be productive unless we had the list of all of the documents that are sought to be tendered plus some indication of what the relevance is so that we could form a view, otherwise we would just be sitting at the Chamber staff reading documents for the first time and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not reading document, but what -- first of all, Chamber staff would, I think, explain further what our concerns are. I've been very brief on it at this very moment. And perhaps to talk about possible solutions of it. And I think during this short conversation we already -- I already noticed that Mr. Jordash said, We have 300 documents and we want to establish this and this and this. Now, first of all, that -- then, of course, we would have to know whether these are all police reports or what's the origin of these documents. And if we have two or three origins then we can more or less structure the issues which are addressed by the bar table motion. And then, of course, the next step is whether we really then need a bar table motion or whether we could address those matters in other ways such as by agreeing on what is factually found. But for the Chamber to receive notice that the parties agree that in July 1994 this unit arrested A, B, or C, or 25 members of paramilitary group so and so, and that they have been detained and that they were brought before the court or they were released after 30 days, that is for the Chamber easier to handle than to get one document of 80 pages in which a lot of other matters are discussed as well and where we have to find out what exactly in those documents you want to bring to our attention. That's, of course, the kind of concerns we have. I suggest that to -- or to discuss the general issues that you invite Mr. Nilsson for the first meeting, not yet going through the documents themselves but just to see where the real problem for the Chamber is. And, of course, the Chamber finally, if it's flooded by documents which were not introduced in a normal way, of course we, at a certain moment, we may also use our discretion in what to admit and what not to admit. That's a matter. We have limits, of course, to our capacity as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution accepts that proposal. I have one brief issue related to this witness if I might raise now so people can think about it over the break. There is a -- in my re-direct examination there's a matter that's been raised by Mr. Jordash that there is an audiotape that was also recovered with the Mladic notebooks that I would like the witness to listen to. I only seek to deal with a short portion of it, but it's 30 minutes long. So what I'm proposing is the following: Have Mr. Laugel preparing the audio file, I will present my colleagues with the transcript, and I'm asking everyone to consider the propriety of allowing the witness to listen to the 30 minute tape overnight so that I can take him directly to the portion that I want to. And he has a sense of the entire context of the -- or the context of the entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'd like to see the transcript first, if I may, before making a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That will be here before the -- sometime during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we'll hear from you later today, that. We'll take a break. And we resume at ten minutes -- no, no, we can take the shorter break - quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just want to -- we don't have a B/C/S version of 1D05283, but if that could be brought up to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you about Nenad Kajkut. And before I do, I want to correct something that I said earlier, which was that your sighting of Simatovic as a Red Beret wasn't in 1993, it was in 1994; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995. I believe it was on the 22nd of February somewhere near Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Nenad Kajkut gave an interview to the OTP in October 2007, and this, it relates, Mr. Milovanovic, to the testimony you've given about the lack of Red Berets, and Kajkut says -- told the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3 of this document and the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He says that at the end of September he -- in 1991 he received a draft for mobilisation, he became a military policeman in the 5th Krajina Corps, which later became the 1st Krajina Corps, and then -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Groome is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just looking at this document. It doesn't appear to be an Office of the Prosecutor document. It doesn't have an ERN, doesn't have a memo form. It doesn't identify the person who spoke to this person. It's a person whose name I've never heard of before. Could I ask for some information before we make representations that it's an OTP interview? I'd like an opportunity to be able to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Actually, I think I've made an error. It's not to the Prosecution. It's a statement he gave, I think, to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we all know that if statements are taken for the purposes of this Tribunal, Mr. Jordash, that in order to be admitted as evidence it should be -- it should be introduced under Rule 92 bis, ter, quater, or quinquies. Apparently this statement has been taken for those purpose, so therefore I think it would be preferable first to ask the witness about the subject matter you would like to deal with. And if you then want to -- if there's any reason to do so, if you then want to put to him what someone else said, you can do that. But the statement in itself seems not to be very suitable for admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let -- Your Honour, okay, yes, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me put it directly because I'm also running out of time, Mr. Milovanovic. But Nenad Kajkut, I suggest, belonged to or was the commander of a group of Red Berets in Banja Luka subordinated to the CSB of Banja Luka. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I was in Macedonia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And he had this group, I suggest, which existed in Banja Luka or in that and around that terrain until 1995 at least? Is that something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, shouldn't we first ask: Do you know a person by the name of Nenad Kajkut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm familiar with a family name. I know some people by that name from around Banja Luka, but I've never heard of Nenad Kajkut before. I don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I have on the screen, please, P2531.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I return now to the Mladic diary and a meeting on the 9th of November, 1993, in which it's said that Milosevic, Lilic, Sainovic, Perisic, Sokolovic, Stojsic, Stanisic, Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Mladic, Hadzic, Begovic, Martic, Novakovic, and Rakic took part. And Milosevic, in the first -- this is page 19 of the -- sorry, this is page 1 of the English. And Milosevic makes the comment that at the first heading: "We co-ordinate based on the army line, Mladic, Perisic, and Novakovic." Would you agree with Milosevic's assessment of the co-ordination between the VRS and the Government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting, so I didn't know what was discussed. Therefore, I don't know what I should agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, from your experience in the VRS and the Main Staff and the supplies from the Serbian government and the military activities in Bosnia under the auspices of the VRS, would you agree that the co-ordination was based on the army line as opposed to other lines such as the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I would kindly ask you to separate two things. Are you asking me about the co-ordination of the armies of the neighbouring states, the coordination of the MUP organisations, or the coordination between the MUP and the army? I really don't know what to deal with first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, what I'm getting at is this: That you, the VRS, were not co-ordinating with the Ministry of Interior of Serbia in relation to combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no co-ordination with the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia. There was no co-ordination with the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska either. If the supreme commander attached a unit to us, for example, a special police unit or specials, that unit had to be placed under the command of the local commander of the army of Republika Srpska. There was no need for any co-ordination between the Ministry of the Interior and the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we move to page 8 of this document, we can see a suggestion by Sokolovic in November of 1993, at number 16, where Sokolovic suggests or he notes that the president has said that: "There is a feeling of empty space in the RS MUP, a specific man with his obligations should be there." Were you aware of the feeling of discontent that the Serbian MUP was still not co-ordinating and the suggestion that the Serbian MUP should, therefore, have somebody placed within the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Looking at the entry by Sokolovic, and I'm suggesting that there was content -- discontent at this late stage, November 1993, that the Serbian MUP was not playing any role with the RS MUP and so Sokolovic made a suggestion that the Serbian MUP place a specific man within the RS MUP, and I'm asking if you are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that person was ever appointed. I was at the meeting so I suppose I should have heard that, but I don't remember. This is what I'm reading, and there's no reason why I should not believe words on paper, but I don't really know whether that person was ever appointed. As far as I know, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at this point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, shouldn't we first -- the text is rather ambiguous, isn't it? "There is a feeling of empty space in the Republika Srpska MUP. A specific man with his obligations should be there." Whose obligations we are talking about seems to be unclear from the text itself. What these obligations are seems to be unclear as well. From where he should come seems to be unclear as well. So to say that we do not know whether he have [sic] ever appointed requires that we have at least an understanding of what this line is about. Could you give us or could you confirm what the -- the understanding you had about the text which appears before us, a text which was spoken, at least that's how it is reported by Mr. Sokolovic. Could you tell us: What kind of a person are we talking about? Would that be a Republic of Serbia MUP men? Or do you have any recollection of the context which could remove some of the ambiguities of this text, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That text, especially the second sentence, doesn't make sense to me because Sokolovic is neither suggesting nor providing a solution. He is only invoking a statement by the president, and he probably means Milosevic, that one should have a personal vision of what the president put forward. Now, who should have that personal vision, whether he or me or the other participants of the meeting or the MUP of the Republic of Serbia or Republika Srpska, I really can't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move to another topic. I was going to take you through the diaries in relation to Operation Breza. But to save time I just want to have you explain what Operation Breza was, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I think it would assist the witness if you would ask him first of all when the operation took place, where the operation took place, what the purpose of the operation was, so that we can work focussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you aware of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise we might have a historical explanation of operations in general and then in specific terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When -- are you aware of Operation Breza, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Breza 94 operation. It was carried out in September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How long did it go on for?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a failed operation by the VRS. I don't think it lasted even ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was its objective, please?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the operation was for the VRS to cross the Una river between Novi Grad and Krupa to take Cazin, or, rather, to take Bihac from the east. It was a personnel operation designed without any plan by General Mladic who started to implement it under the command of General Talic of the 1st Krajina Corps. It became a failure as soon as it started actually. On the first day around Novi Grad in just one night we lost 92 men, several vehicles, mainly commander vehicles, of the Main Staff were captured, as well as vehicles of the 1st Krajina Corps, and the operation was cut short.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say personal operation, or personnel operation, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise to the president of the Trial Chamber but I have to take a couple of minutes to explain how this operation occurred. The Main Staff was supposed to carry out an inspection of various corps, and General Mladic took it upon himself to inspect the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps in the west of Republika Srpska. My job was to inspect the eastern part, or, rather, the corps on the eastern front, the Herzegovina Corps and the Eastern Bosnia Corps. We set out each in his own way, and one evening Mladic called me in Bijeljina and ordered me to come back to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I need to just cut you short, I'm sorry, but I need to move swiftly. Who supplied Operation Breza -- and I think it was actually called Operation Breza 1994 - who supplied Operation Breza with logistics, ammunition, weapons?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at the outset that the troops went into offensive unprepared, what we in the army call straight from the trenches. It was an idea of General Mladic. He went into it with what he had on the front line, and he reckoned that I would send him the guard brigade from the Main Staff and I was supposed to take three units from around Sarajevo and around Treskavica and send them to Krajina, which was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you receive for that operation any logistics or weapons or ammunitions supply from the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge nothing was requested and nothing was supplied. General Mladic wanted it to be a surprise attack against the 5th Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree that the strategic objective of that operation was to assist Abdic to return his people, the refugees, back to Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that General Mladic was not thinking about that during those days because a couple of days earlier Abdic's army had been defeated and the population had been crammed into collection centres and camps. He wasn't trying to get Abdic back into power. But almost a year before that General Talic kept talking him into the idea that the 1st Corps has enough resources to deal with the problems of the Cazin Krajina on its own. The Cazin Krajina is an area facing Croatia, bordering on Croatia, and it was never within the sphere of interests of Republika Srpska. At the Assembly session that we discussed yesterday of the 12th of May, the boundaries were defined loosely as the Una river, the Sava river, the Drina River, and the Neretva river. So if Mladic had succeeded, we would have had to bring back the army as we had brought it back later from Bjelasnica and Igman. But Mladic went into this offensive of his own accord and it ended the way it ended. Nobody, not Mladic and not Talic, knew that the Muslim army had not complied with a decision of the UN Security Council, I don't know which number, which proclaimed the Bihac region a protected area. UNPROFOR notified us that the 5th Corps had been disarmed. However, in those 18 months that corps was not only disarmed, it was resupplied and it became a big corps of 2.000 men with state-of-the-art equipment. And they even had the so-called Singapore rifles, the dream of every soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You said it was not in the sphere of interest of Republika Srpska. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly of Republika Srpska defined the borders of the then-Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina along those four rivers I named, Una, Sava, Drina, and Neretva. Anything beyond those lines would mean aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So this, then, operation was outside of the strategic objectives of the VRS; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What, then, motivated Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was Operation Breza 94 a kind of precursor to Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a consequence of the Pauk operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But Operation Breza 94 came before Pauk, didn't it? Are you saying Pauk was a consequence of Breza?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Pauk was the consequence of the Breza operation. I misspoke, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So, again, Pauk, then, do you categor-- characterise that in the same way you would Breza, which is that it was an operation outside of the strategic objectives of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Something else happened in the meantime. When I said that Pauk was a consequence of the Breza operation, Breza was caused by the 5th Muslim Corps and it was decided that they were a failure. And the very next month, on the 23rd of October, that corps aggressed Republika Srpska by crossing Mount Grmec. They crossed Una river and with seven days occupied around 250.000 square kilometres of the territory of Republika Srpska. So the VRS had to take that land back, that is, to mount that famous counter-attack against Bihac that I was unlucky enough to lead. The counter-strike took 16 days of offensive. We pushed back the Muslims to the other side of the Una river and that was taken advantage of by the Serbian Army of Krajina so they took offensive actions against the 5th Corps again, and we meant to crush that corps by joint effort. I drew that conclusion on the 8th of November, of which I spoke in my last testimony, when I was tricked into coming to Plitvice where they tried to persuade me to co-operate with the Serbian Army of Krajina with part of my forces to revive for a while the army of Fikret Abdic. I did not have authorisation from the Main Staff or the Supreme Command to be involved in those negotiations and even less did I have authorisation to give them I don't know how many men and 5.000 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, at the beginning of this answer there's one explanation missing provided by the General about the motivation of the commander of the 5th Corps to take the action that he had taken. Just the first few lines are incomplete. And I believe what's missing is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us the transcript page and line, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 65, lines 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you were asked whether you could categorise Pauk in the same way as you would categorize Breza in that it was an operation outside of the strategic objectives of the VRS. Now, for us the answer starts with: "No. Something else happened in the meantime." And it follows then, Mr. Petrovic? Or is it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the bit. That's the passage that's incomplete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then you apparently added something, where our transcript reads: "When I said that Pauk was a consequence of the Breza operation, Breza was caused by the 5th Muslim corps," et cetera. But apparently something is missing from your answer. Could you very briefly indicate what may be missing here. And apparently it has to do something with the motivation of the commander of the 5th Corps to take the action he had taken. Could you please repeat what you said in that context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. I'll try to be brief. The 5th Corps crushed, from 19 to the 21st of August, the army of Fikret Abdic. General Mladic thought that he could punish the 5th Corps, not because they crushed Fikret Abdic, but because they had armed themselves; whereas they were supposed to be disarmed, under the decision of the UN Security Council. Neither general evaluated properly the strength of the 5th Corps, and they failed. And then the 5th Corps mounted Grmec 94 to punish VRS and to take these 250.000 square kilometres. Before that, throughout the war, they had fought in encirclement. But they broke out of that encirclement and faced the VRS. The VRS mounted a counter-strike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you here. Exceptionally I'll invite Mr. Petrovic to ask a question of the following kind: "Did I hear you say ..." and then you repeat what you heard the witness said and which doesn't appear on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. General, did I hear you say that the commander of the 5th Corps thought and felt that the VRS was weak in that area and moved into offensive action into the territory held at that time by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then now on the record. Mr. Jordash, you certainly are aware that in 15 minutes from now you've used six hours. That is the five hours plus the one granted by Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I'll finish in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we turn, please, to 65 ter 1413, Supreme Defence Council minutes, 28th Session, held on the 2nd of November, 1994. Could we have page 5 of the English and 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just to orientate ourselves, perhaps we should just look at the first page, sorry, the second page, where we get a list of those who attended this session. Which, to speed things up: Lilic, Milosevic, Momir Bulatovic, Kontic, Perisic, Krivosija. And at page 5 of the English and 4 of the B/C/S we have, it seems, a discussion about Bosnia by Perisic. And just to -- just to -- just to orientate ourselves, November 1994 was when Pauk began; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Operation Pauk was only being discussed on the 8th of November, and this session was on the 2nd of November. On November 3rd I went into that attack across Mount Grmec.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So Pauk started, then, in December of 1994? It was at the end of 1994, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Sometime in mid-1994, a couple of days before the conclusion of so-called Carter's cease-fire, on 23rd December Pauk was cut short and continued again only in the spring of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, if you look at what Perisic is talking about in relation to Bosnia, a third of the way down the page, when he announces: "Gentlemen presidents, I would like to briefly introduce you to the situation in Bosnia. The Muslim Croatian forces have started a general offensive, aiming at cutting off the western part of the Republika Srpska in the Bihac Bugojno direction." Just a bit further down: "Therefore they have started with the offensive. They have started with the offensive in the direction Bjelasnica-Gorazde and vice versa so that they merge and make passage in this enclave. Furthermore, they are significantly progressing towards the corridor. So far they have occupied 843 square kilometres since September the 1st. In total, the Serbs had to evacuate around 15.750 citizens from that area." Do you agree with that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm seeing this evaluation for the first time and I don't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What do you disagree with?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't agree with the evaluation about the Muslim offensive from Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica towards Gorazde and from Gorazde towards Sarajevo because between these two features there is the city of Sarajevo. Second, there was no need for the Muslims to attack from Gorazde towards Sarajevo because they had got a corridor between Sarajevo and Gorazde through Carter's cease-fire, and that corridor of 120 square kilometres still exists to date. Now, where Perisic took these figures on losses, I don't know. But I said that a date later I mounted my counter-attack across Mount Grmec towards Bihac. So I think this evaluation by Perisic is irrelevant to that time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about the beginning of that paragraph where he talks of a general offensive aimed at cutting off the western part of Republika Srpska and Bihac; is that what you're saying didn't exist?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of the evaluation is all right. The offensive of the 5th Corps and the Croatian army from the Bihac region towards Bugojno, and the Muslims were also preparing an offensive of their 7th Corps, I believe, from the wider area of Bugojno towards Bihac, they wanted to link up those forces so that the 5th Corps would finally break out of encirclement. And there was a strategic Muslim idea throughout the war to create a green transversal across Sandzak, Sarajevo, Bugojno, and Bihac. Now, I don't have to explain what the green transversal is. It's a historical fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move on as swiftly as we can to page 6 of the English and 5 of the B/C/S, and it's Milosevic speaking. Sorry, it's not, it's Perisic speaking again. And if we then go over the page in the English to 7 and B/C/S 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I'm interested in the section where Perisic talks, halfway down the page of the English. And he starts to talk about the impact on the FRY safety as a result of the continuation of war by the Bosnian Serbs by the VRS. And he -- if you would read the section where it starts off with saying: "Firstly the situation in the FRY army."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of these discussions happening in the -- in Belgrade amongst the Serbian government about basically the disastrous consequences of the continuation of the war in Bosnia by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know and I was not interested at the time what was going on at Pale. I said that I launched my counter-attack against 22.000 Muslim fighters, having already lost 6.000 of my fighters. I read Perisic's evaluation on the previous page with a reference to the 7th Corps, and that is in keeping with my previous claim that the 5th and the 7th Corps were supposed to link up their forces in the western part of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 23 of the English and page 22 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's Slobodan Milosevic. He's presenting his view about the current situation in Bosnia. And he notes: [As read] "The fact that the worst situation is there is unfortunately the best argument that a disastrous mistake was made when the peace accord was rejected. It is a direct consequence. That night when we talked with them in Dobanovci for the last time, Momir is here, Momcilo is here, we precisely pointed out such tendency and presented what would happen. They proved that the peace accord should not have been accepted. Unfortunately, that proof costs now, 3.000. No way, that is not true. It is much more. No one should have died in Gorazde, not in Gorazde, not in the corridor, not in Nisic Plateau, not in Grabez or the Una valley, Kupres, et cetera. But if the price for proving the decision of the Pale leadership to reject the peace accord to be right is to have so many people get killed, and unfortunately which resulted in losing the territory and not conquering it, then I really do not know what the logic means, what the justice means. What is a smart thing to do?" And then if we go over the page to page 24 of the English and stay with page 22 of the B/C/S, Milosevic says: "The peace accord is still on the table luckily. If the map changes due to the significant combat activities of the Muslim-Croatian coalition, they will not accept that plan." Were you aware that Milosevic and the Serb leadership took the view, at this point in time onwards, that if you, the Bosnian Serbs, lost territory it would mean that the peace agreement would continue to be rejected by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Serbian government's official policy, and we see, I suggest, it expressed through Milosevic at that point, were you aware that they took the view that the loss of territory by the Bosnian Serbs would mean that they would not accept the peace agreement which was on the table?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. But I agree and I understand why the leadership of Republika Srpska did not accept that accord, because that would confirm the status quo. And we have to bear in mind that in the short space of seven days we had lost 250.000 square kilometres of our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And causing a massive refugee crisis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That refugee crisis was particularly prominent on Mount Grmec. But for 57 days we managed to have the population return. They returned to destroyed homes, but they did return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: One last part of this and then I'll finish there, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 33 of the English and 30 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Milosevic expresses his view once again, noting that: [As read] "And all that happens after so much suffering. We endured everything, we went through all the sanctions, and we came to the point where the entire international community says, All right, you are not the aggressors. Half of Bosnia and Herzegovina is yours and you have the right to merge with Serbia and Montenegro. They say no we will -- and we will take even more by force. We will prolong the war. That is what I call complete madness." And Bulatovic then notes: "They have already lost 850 square kilometres of the territory." Was that view communicated to you through Mladic or any other Bosnian Serb leader at the time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we still talking about the 2nd November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody communicated anything to me. Karadzic told me sometime in mid-December that Jimmy Carter should arrive and that I should be prepared for defence, because I discussed the issue of Bihac with him and whether I should enter Bihac or not, because the issue of Bihac was a political rather than a military issue. As a soldier, I had every right to enter Bihac and to attack the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the witness, by the first line, has answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got nothing further. Thank you, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to start your further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's try and use the remaining time to clarify some things, to shed some light on your previous testimony. First of all, just awhile ago we talked about the beginning of the Operation Pauk and it says on page 68 that that happened sometime in mid-1994. Can you please repeat and tell us when the Operation Pauk actually started.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Pauk had a different name. Its original name was Stit 1994. Sometime in mid-December, on the eve of Jimmy Carter's arrival, after the four-month peace accord was signed, Operation Pauk was shelved. However, on the 13th of January, 1995, the 1st Corps violated the peace accord that was supposed to last for four months. It launched another attack on the VRS and the Serbian Army of Krajina. I'm not sure about the latter. Operation Pauk was rekindled sometime in mid-February or, to be more precise, on the 12th or the 13th February. At least according to the information I received from Nikola Koljevic, the deputy prime minister of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, on the record on page 74, line 9, it says that the 1st Corps violated the peace accord. Could you please shed some light on that. Who was it who violated the peace accord?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The peace accord that was supposed to last for four months, is that what you're asking me? The peace accord was violated by General Atif Dudakovic on the eve of the Orthodox new year which was on the 13th of January. He slaughtered four of our fighters in a bunker. They had sent several of our fighters to congratulate the Orthodox new year to the Serbs. I suppose that they had been drinking together and then they slaughtered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, just tell me who Dudakovic was; was he the commander of a corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of the 5th Corps of the so-called Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Earlier today and yesterday you mentioned the airfield at Ravna Romanija, i.e., an attempt to build an airport there. Are you referring to the attempts to build an airfield near Sokolac at the foot of Mount Romanija?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Close to the cross-road -- cross-roads of Sokolac-Rogatica-Pale roads, in the so-called Glasinac [phoen] field.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Earlier today and yesterday you spoke about the basic training of recruits in the VRS. You said that it lasted for three months and then for the first eight months no single recruit would be allowed to go to the front line and be engaged in combat. You said that that training would last for at least eight months before they had the necessary skills.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was something else that I should have added and that is that they could have been engaged if they were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, as a soldier with years of experience would you be able to tell us whether a soldier can be trained within the scope of, let's say, a fortnight? What such training be adequate? Would it make any sense?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a short training would be a crime against such a soldier. Basic training should not last less than three and a half months. Within a fortnight you can only teach him how to fire a bullet, but not how to aim at a target or defend himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. As for those recruits who served in the army, how long did it take for them to renew the skills that they had acquired during their compulsory military service? I'm talking about your experience and the experience of warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, we are spending ages and ages on what seems to be training not at an adequate level. Should we know exactly what you would have learned or how much time it would take to regain your skills, et cetera, whether that would be handling rifles or mortars or tanks or airplanes, and then to go in all those details; or do you want to address our attention to the fact that this witness, as supported by some of the documents, is of the opinion that training of recruits was inadequate due to the circumstances? If that is what you want to draw our attention to, then I think you together with Mr. Jordash have been very effective already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I note the time. Should I continue or should we break now and resume tomorrow, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we should -- we should adjourn. But I'd first like the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. Mr. Milovanovic, the same instruction applies as I gave you yesterday, that is, that you should not speak or communicate with anyone about your testimony either already given now or in past or still to be given in the days to come. And we'll further discuss how and when we'll be able to conclude your examination. Would you please follow the usher. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I have two questions actually. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When do we continue tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning at 9.00. Yes, I should have told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, secondly, am I supposed to go on reading and finish reading the third binder of documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do not know what Mr. Petrovic would like you to further read. What I do know is that the Prosecution would like to give you a transcript of an audio recording. And that was how many pages, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it's about seven pages, Your Honour. Ten pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome has 7 -- a 10-page document for you. Mr. Petrovic, any wishes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. I'll try and deal with all the documents and parts thereof here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Milovanovic, you have some time to recover, only ten pages to deal with, at least if you're willing to assist the Prosecution by reading them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, and a 30-minute audiotape of the transcript of the pages is what I proposed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I thought there was a transcript of that audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is a transcript, Your Honour, but I don't know whether the Chamber wants me to address my proposed questions for the witness in his hearing. I don't think there's anything that's going prejudice his listening to the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I have no problems. So what you say is you have 10 pages of transcripts and you have an audio attached to the same matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it's an audiotape recovered from the Mladic home. And when the witness listens to it, if he could assist us in identifying the voices, approximate the time that this may be, and there's a reference or several references to a Manojlo, whether he can tell us whether that's a reference to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milovanovic, apart from reading the ten pages, you're also invited -- And I take it, Mr. Groome, that you provide the equipment necessary for listening?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have it here in court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have it here in court, yes. You're also invited to listen to a 30-minutes' audio recording, and some specific questions were already mentioned by Mr. Groome. While listening could you try to identify who is speaking; could you try to identify what is -- will be the approximate time of recording; and where reference is made to Manojlo, could you please see whether you can tell us whether that is a reference to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, so the record is complete: This is ERN number T001-2432, and it is side A of a two-sided cassette tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Side A is the side you are expected to listen to. Is that clear, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear. Maybe I could listen to the tape now? Maybe I don't even have to go to the hotel and then return from the hotel to listen to the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am -- no, but I think you will be provided with all the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have it. And if VWS doesn't mind allowing him to listen to it in their office, the Prosecution would have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, I mean, there's recorder on which the tape can be played?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the recorder and the headset here, as well as the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You can have everything, you can take it to your hotel, you don't have to come back to listen to it because you get all the equipment you need. But if you prefer to listen to it now, that's fine as well. Then please ask VWS to give you a place where to listen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then would you please follow the usher, and the usher would provide you with the text and the equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to verify whether there's any way that we conclude the testimony of this witness before the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Petrovic still abides by his one-hour limit, I think we can -- we will certainly finish before the weekend, if there are no procedural matters that would delay us. I think I would use about two hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's considerably less than the four or five hours you indicated before. So then we'll try -- Mr. Petrovic, we'll be rather strict on your time tomorrow, that is, 53 minutes left, and then two hours for the Prosecution, which leaves some time for further questions. I urge the parties to see whether we really can finish by a quarter to 2.00. Then we adjourn. And we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 8th of December, at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of December, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.51 p.m.,
